structure.title: II. Institutional Background and Plant Productivity
VI. How Do Acquirers Improve Productive Efficiency?
VIII. Concluding Remarks and Data Availability

observations.statement: The paper names its main estimand as an average treatment effect on the treated for the acquisitions that were actually proposed, distinguishing it explicitly from a hypothetical average treatment effect under random assignment.

Causal interpretation is argued to rest on treatment producing a discontinuous change in plant behavior while unobserved selection trends would be comparatively gradual, combined with flat pre-acquisition coefficients supporting parallel trends.

The authors discuss a reverse-causality threat in which acquirers might anticipate future efficiency gains (for example from an upcoming manager departure) and buy in anticipation, and describe a targeted check meant to speak to this scenario.

A stable-unit-treatment-value threat is named explicitly: never-treated units competing in the same markets as treated units could be indirectly affected through competitive spillovers, motivating a market-restricted matching design as a check.

The identification strategy is described as combining a static specification with pre- and post-acquisition indicators against a difference-in-differences comparison group, plus a separate dynamic monthly event-study specification centered on the acquisition month.

The sample is built by combining several named agency and vendor sources: federal regulatory filings, an environmental hourly monitoring program, an energy statistics agency, a reliability-organization outage database, a commercial market-intelligence vendor, and a weather data vendor.

Different component datasets cover different windows: the core production and ownership data run over roughly two decades beginning in the early 2000s, while the personnel data and the outage/maintenance data each cover shorter, non-overlapping subperiods.

The paper walks through a sequential exclusion chain from the full generator and transaction universe to the estimation sample, explaining the substantive reason for each step, including removing cogenerators, non-majority stake changes, and ownership changes tied to regulatory restructuring rather than acquisitions.

The unit of analysis is stated to be the individual generator rather than the plant or firm, justified on the grounds that generators within the same plant can differ in production profile, maintenance schedule, and retirement timing.

Two separate record-linkage procedures are described: an algorithmic match between anonymized outage-event records and the production dataset's generator identifiers, and a name-based match of plant personnel records to professional-network profiles to recover education and title.

Capital-expenditure and non-fuel-cost data are noted to be available only for the subset of plants that report to the federal regulator as major electric utilities, a narrower and lower-frequency dataset than the main hourly production data.

The primary efficiency outcome is defined as the inverse of heat rate, the ratio of fuel heat content to electricity output, and this ratio is log-transformed for use as the dependent variable in the regression specifications.

Acquisition (treatment) is defined as a change in the firm holding the majority ownership share of a generator, with a stated tie-break rule for cases without a clear majority holder, and split into two subtypes depending on whether the direct or only the indirect owner changes.

For the structural production-function analysis, ramp rate is constructed as the hour-to-hour change in a generator's output scaled by its capacity, and enters as a control alongside ambient temperature and humidity in the heat-rate function.

Heterogeneity indicators used to interact with the treatment dummies, such as serial-acquirer status, relative acquirer and generator size, and a cross-market flag, are constructed from observable transaction and firm characteristics, with the construction details deferred to an appendix section.

The main efficiency table builds up the preferred specification column by column, adding successive blocks of fixed effects and controls before presenting the preferred column and then splitting that same preferred specification by acquisition subtype in the final columns.

Regression tables report the model R-squared, an observation count, and separate counts of treated and comparison units, and the table notes state both the standard-error type and the clustering level rather than leaving this only to the main text.

For outcome variables measured in levels rather than logs, such as generation, utilization, and outages, the corresponding table reports the pre-acquisition mean of the dependent variable so that the reader can benchmark magnitudes against a baseline level.

The main tables carry no observation weights; a capacity-weighted version of the baseline specification is reported only as a separate robustness check rather than as a column of the main results table.

Standard errors are clustered at the acquisition (transaction) level throughout the main efficiency and performance tables; this level is stated repeatedly in table notes but the choice of clustering level itself is not argued for beyond naming it.

Two figures reporting related but secondary regressions, the manager-turnover event study and the acquirer/target productivity-level comparison, cluster standard errors at the plant level rather than at the acquisition level used elsewhere, without an explicit statement of why the level differs.

Pre-trends are shown through a dynamic event-study plot in which coefficients for the pre-acquisition months are visually flat and their confidence intervals cross zero; no separate formal joint-significance test of the pre-period coefficients is reported alongside the plot.

Two placebo-style checks are used to probe unobserved confounding: re-running the design on non-majority ownership changes that fall below the acquisition threshold, and estimating efficiency effects of manager turnover occurring without any accompanying ownership change.
observations.locator: Section IV.A text and Section VII, Placebo tests

observations.statement: For the structural heat-rate-curve comparison, a bootstrap-based confidence band around the difference between the pre- and post-acquisition curves is constructed and reported in an online-appendix figure to support the claim that the curve shift is not noise.
observations.locator: Section V.B, referencing an online-appendix figure

observations.statement: Possible spillovers onto comparison units are addressed diagnostically in two ways: an appendix matching design that pairs each treated unit only with units from different markets, and a robustness sample restricted to transactions too small to plausibly move market-wide outcomes.

A staggered-adoption-robust estimator is applied as an alternative to the two-way-fixed-effects specification, addressing concerns that comparisons could implicitly use already-treated units as controls; the paper summarizes the result as consistent with the baseline and defers the full output to the appendix.

A dedicated robustness section runs the baseline regression under a series of alternative choices, including a different data frequency, an expanded acquisition sample, capacity weighting, an alternative generation measure, and a restricted post-restructuring sample period, each summarized in a short paragraph pointing to specific appendix tables and figures.

A matched difference-in-differences check pairs each treated generator with several comparison units drawn from a different market but sharing fuel type and technology, chosen via a distance metric on capacity and age, as an alternative to the regression-based comparison group.

A count-data estimator is used as an alternative functional form for outcome variables that take the value zero for some generator-weeks, addressing a concern that the levels specification for those outcomes could be sensitive to functional-form choice.
observations.locator: Section IV.A, footnote on outcome estimation

observations.statement: Heterogeneity across generator, firm, and transaction characteristics is estimated through interaction terms added to the baseline specification rather than through fully separate subsample regressions, and the authors explicitly caveat that this heterogeneity does not by itself establish a causal interpretation.
observations.quote: these findings do not establish causality

observations.statement: The split between ownership changes at the direct (subsidiary) versus indirect (parent) level is explicitly tied back to the paper's broader argument that direct operational control by the new owner is what drives efficiency gains, rather than reported as a standalone descriptive fact.

An additional heterogeneity cut by market and regulatory characteristics, comparing organized-market, high-acquisition-activity, and deregulated-state generators, is placed in a footnote with results pointed to an appendix table rather than appearing in the main heterogeneity table.

Two candidate mechanisms, productive efficiency and dynamic efficiency, are each given an explicit testable prediction derived from a Leontief production-function microfoundation before being tested empirically, rather than being motivated only after seeing the reduced-form results.

Manager turnover, capital expenditures, non-fuel input costs, and maintenance-event probability are each analyzed as intermediate outcomes meant to separate an operational-improvement channel from a capital-investment channel underlying the productive-efficiency mechanism.

Several mechanism findings, including the manager-turnover results and the market-characteristic heterogeneity split, are explicitly qualified by the authors as suggestive rather than conclusive on their own.

The capital-investment channel is argued against jointly through a precision-based bound on the estimated capital-expenditure coefficient and a timing argument that meaningful capital projects would take longer to implement and cause more downtime than what is observed shortly after acquisition.

The average efficiency effect is benchmarked against a separately estimated statistic for typical organic within-generator productivity growth among never-acquired units, used to argue that the acquisition effect is large relative to the industry's baseline trend.

The estimated efficiency gain is translated into an implied cumulative emissions reduction under stated simplifying assumptions, and that reduction is then re-expressed in an intuitive equivalent unit, an explicit back-of-envelope calculation rather than a formal welfare estimate.

The total estimated efficiency gain is decomposed into shares attributable to the productive-efficiency and dynamic-efficiency mechanisms, with an explicit caveat that the two shares need not sum exactly to the total because of estimation noise.

The authors state plainly that ownership changes are not random and that unobservable factors could influence efficiency independent of acquisitions, framing this as a caveat that robustness checks can address only partially rather than eliminate.

A limitation is stated that the magnitude of the estimated efficiency effect might not extend to industries whose production technology or acquisition motives differ substantially from electricity generation, even as the authors argue the mechanism evidence carries broader lessons.

The authors caveat that their preferred estimand, an effect on the treated for acquisitions that were actually proposed and approved, does not directly support a counterfactual analysis of how outcomes would change under a different antitrust policy regime.

The efficiency measure is explicitly noted to capture fuel efficiency only, not a broader total-factor-productivity concept that accounts for non-fuel inputs, and the authors flag that longer-horizon heat-rate gains could trade off against unobserved mechanical wear that their multi-year window cannot fully capture.
observations.locator: Section II.C footnote and Section IV.B

observations.statement: The authors are explicit that the electricity-generation setting was chosen specifically because it offers physical quantity data and a homogeneous product that make clean measurement possible, acknowledging this as a deliberate trade-off against broader industry generalizability.

The sample is explicitly scoped to the period following the industry's deregulation wave and deliberately excludes ownership changes tied to that earlier restructuring episode, distinguishing the paper's post-deregulation setting from prior divestiture-era studies of the same industry.

Dynamic treatment-effect estimates are consistently presented as coefficient plots with confidence intervals across the main dynamic-efficiency result and two mechanism analyses, rather than as coefficient tables, making the event-study figure the paper's default way to show timing.

Main regression tables report coefficients with standard errors in parentheses but no significance stars, relying on the reader to interpret precision from the reported standard errors, while each table's notes state the sample, fixed effects, and clustering level.

A single summary-statistics table presents generator, firm, and transaction characteristics across several sample-restriction columns side by side, letting the reader see how each successive sample restriction changes the composition of the data rather than using one table per restriction.

Supplementary tables and figures are consistently labeled with an appendix prefix and collected in a separate online appendix, cross-referenced from the main text by that label whenever a robustness check or additional diagnostic is mentioned.
observations.locator: throughout, e.g. footnote 27 and Section VII

observations.statement: The introduction previews the paper's headline quantitative findings and mechanism conclusions ahead of the corresponding sections, and closes with a dedicated contribution paragraph that situates the paper against three distinct literatures.

Institutional background and the construction of the efficiency measure are presented before the data section, which in turn precedes the formal statement of the empirical specification, so background and data come before the identification strategy is formalized.

The paper follows a main-result-first structure, placing all mechanism analysis after the headline efficiency and heterogeneity results, and collects every robustness check into its own dedicated section positioned after the mechanism sections and before the conclusion.

Most robustness results, several diagnostic checks, and additional heterogeneity splits are documented only in a lettered online appendix referenced by section, table, or figure label throughout the main text rather than reproduced in the body of the paper.

A dedicated data-availability statement at the end of the paper cites a specific archived repository entry hosting the code, data, and instructions the authors state are sufficient to replicate the numerical results in both the main text and the online appendixes.

The main text itself does not name the statistical software or econometrics package used to implement the regressions; any such detail is left to the cited replication package rather than stated in the article body.
observations.locator: Data Availability statement and Section IV

observations.statement: The ownership and transaction dataset is built by cross-referencing a commercial market-intelligence vendor's records with company press releases and news articles specifically to correct known misclassification problems in ownership databases, such as name changes or corporate restructurings being mistaken for acquisitions.
observations.locator: Section III.A, Ownership and acquisition data

observations.statement: The outage and maintenance dataset is stated to have been obtained through a data-sharing agreement with the reliability organization that maintains it, an access procedure distinct from the otherwise publicly available regulatory and statistical-agency sources used elsewhere.
observations.locator: Section III.A, Maintenance and outage data

concordance.paper_says: Baseline specification is an OLS regression with generator and week fixed effects, pre/post acquisition indicators (eq. 2), and a companion dynamic monthly event-study specification (eq. 3), estimated by what the paper calls a difference-in-differences design.
concordance.card_shows: Recipe card design d1 (method=event_study) and spec s1 (estimator=hdfe_ols, command=feols) traced to table1_heat_rate.R, matching a fixed-effects OLS call with a formula built from an outcome, unit/time controls, and treat_all/treat_post indicators.

concordance.paper_says: Table 2 lists a progression of fixed effects for the preferred column: generator and week fixed effects, state-by-month trends, unit-characteristic-by-month trends (installation year, fuel, technology, capacity bin), and scrubber/environmental-program fixed effects.
concordance.card_shows: Specification s1.fixed_effects is null; the card's evidence trace only captured the feols call and formula string, not the enumerated fixed-effect terms actually substituted into it.

concordance.paper_says: The main text and every main-table note state that standard errors are clustered at the acquisition (transaction) level; two secondary figures instead state plant-level clustering.
concordance.card_shows: s1.se.type is recorded as cluster with the structured cluster_level field left null; the card's free-text se.details notes clustering on a deal_number variable when available and otherwise a plant identifier, consistent with but less precise than the paper's stated acquisition-level clustering.
concordance.note: Structured cluster_level field is null in the card; agreement is based on the card's free-text se.details matching the paper's stated level.

concordance.paper_says: Standard errors are described throughout as clustered (never heteroskedasticity-robust alone, wild-bootstrapped, or randomization-inference based) in the main specifications.
concordance.card_shows: s1.se.type = cluster, traced to the cluster argument of the feols call.

concordance.paper_says: The estimation sample restricts to each generator's first acquisition, excludes cogenerators, non-majority ownership changes, and restructuring-driven ownership changes, and drops acquired generators from the sample a fixed number of years after their first acquisition so post-treatment periods are not used as comparison data.
concordance.card_shows: pipeline.sample_restrictions is an empty list; no sample-restriction steps were captured by the code trace underlying the card.

concordance.paper_says: The baseline specification is described as an unweighted average effect, with a capacity-weighted version presented separately as a robustness check.
concordance.card_shows: s1.weights is null (unknown), with no evidence trace either confirming or contradicting an unweighted baseline.

concordance.paper_says: The preferred specification's controls are described in detail: ambient temperature and humidity, environmental-program participation indicators, and pollution-control-device indicators, layered on top of the fixed-effect trend controls.
concordance.card_shows: s1.controls_summary is null; the card records only the formula string with a generic controls placeholder rather than resolving which variables it contains.

concordance.paper_says: The paper reports a pre-trends event-study figure with flat, insignificant pre-acquisition coefficients as its main design diagnostic, plus placebo checks using minority acquisitions and manager changes without acquisitions.
concordance.card_shows: diagnostics is an empty list; no diagnostic checks were captured in the card's code trace.

concordance.paper_says: Section VII enumerates several robustness checks: alternative data frequency, an expanded acquisition sample, capacity weighting, an alternative generation measure, a restricted post-2010 sample, a matched comparison-group design, a staggered-adoption-robust estimator, and a placebo test.
concordance.card_shows: robustness is an empty list; the card's reading scope covered only one baseline analysis script and did not trace the robustness scripts.

concordance.paper_says: The comparison group for the baseline design is generators never or not-yet acquired; for the structural heat-rate-curve analysis a separate matched control group is constructed from never-acquired generators in different markets with similar capacity, age, fuel, and technology.
concordance.card_shows: d1.comparison_group is null; the design record traced from the code does not specify how the comparison group is constructed.

concordance.paper_says: The main text alone presents six numbered tables and nine numbered figures, with a further set of appendix-only tables and figures referenced throughout Section VII and the footnotes.
concordance.card_shows: outputs.tables lists a single generic table entry (format txt, via the xtable package) traced from one output-writing call, and outputs.figures is empty.
concordance.note: Card coverage is partial (files_read lists four scripts out of an estimated fifty-seven in the repository), so the gap likely reflects incomplete code tracing rather than a discrepancy about what the code actually produces.

gaps: No preregistration, pre-analysis plan, IRB approval, or research-ethics/consent statement appears anywhere in the read main text.
No explicit statement of the statistical software, package, or version used for estimation appears in the main text; this is left to the cited replication package.

No formal joint-significance test (for example an F-test or Wald test) for the pre-acquisition event-study coefficients is reported in the main text; only the plotted coefficients and their individual confidence intervals are shown.
No explicit multiple-testing correction is discussed despite many heterogeneity interactions and secondary-outcome regressions being estimated across Tables 3-6.

The online appendix itself (sections A-F, tables OA-1 through OA-17, figures OA-1 through OA-23) is not part of the extracted text; every appendix-only practice recorded in this note is based on how the main text describes that appendix content, not on directly reading it.

reading.note: Read the full extracted main text front to back (title/abstract through the reference list, pages 1-51), including all main tables, figure captions, and footnotes. The paper's online appendix (sections A-F and the OA-numbered tables/figures it repeatedly cites) is a separate document not included in this text extraction and was not read; observations about appendix content reflect only what the main text says about it.
